p.x:
I'm Nat, and I'm a teenager. I'm fifteen years old. On weekdays, I go to school from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. My favourite subject is art.
After school, I text my friends and we meet at the mall. We like looking at clothes and cool sneakers, but we don't have much money! In the evening, I do my homework. Then, if I have time, I play games online. Gaming is my favourite hobby.
My parents have some rules. I can't use my phone at dinner, and I must be in bed by 10:30. Sometimes I think the rules are too strict, but I know my parents care about me.

p.t: Growing Up in the Digital Age
p.x:
Being a teenager today is very different from twenty years ago. Most teenagers spend hours on social media every day. They share photos, chat with friends and follow celebrities. Many parents worry about screen time and set limits.
Teenagers also want more freedom. They want to hang out with friends at the weekend and stay out late, but many parents set a curfew. If teenagers break the rules, they might get grounded and not be allowed to go out.
Some older teenagers get a part-time job in a café or shop to earn extra money, while younger ones usually receive an allowance from their parents. Teenagers also have their own language: slang words that their parents often don't understand!
Adolescence can be a difficult time. Many teenagers feel self-conscious about their appearance, especially if they have acne or braces. They experience mood swings and may become rebellious. Exam stress is also a big problem, especially before university entrance exams. Some students choose to take a gap year before university to travel or work.
Most of all, teenagers are trying to discover their identity. They want to fit in with their friends but also stand out as individuals. Everything from their first love to an embarrassing moment in class can feel enormously important, and even ordinary conversations can feel awkward.

For a long time, adults explained teenage behaviour simply as the effect of hormones. Recent research in neuroscience, however, has revealed a more complex picture. During puberty and the years that follow, the brain undergoes major reorganisation, and this process continues until the mid-twenties.
The areas of the brain responsible for emotion and reward develop relatively early, while the prefrontal cortex, which controls planning, judgement and self-control, matures later. This imbalance may explain why adolescents are more likely to engage in risk-taking, particularly when their friends are watching. The influence of peers is especially powerful: studies show that teenagers take more risks in experiments when they believe other young people are observing them.
This does not mean that teenagers are simply immature. The same brain flexibility that makes them vulnerable also makes them exceptionally good at learning, adapting and generating new ideas. Many researchers now see adolescence as a period of opportunity rather than merely a problem to be managed. Teenagers who are given appropriate autonomy, with clear limits, often become more confident and mature adults.
Social media adds new challenges. Constant comparison with edited images can damage body image, and online pressures can intensify the generation gap, as parents struggle to understand worlds they did not grow up in. Yet the fundamental experience of coming of age, with its uncertainty, excitement and search for meaning, remains remarkably similar across generations.
